claim: Grid cells fire in sequences that represent rapid trajectories in space.
source: Grid cells fire in sequences that represent rapid trajectories in space.
evidence: This is a general statement about grid cell behavior that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: During locomotion, theta sequences encode sweeps in position starting slightly behind the animal and ending ahead of it.
source: During locomotion, theta sequences encode sweeps in position starting slightly behind the animal and ending ahead of it.
evidence: This statement describes a known property of theta sequences supported by scientific literature.

claim: During quiescence and slow wave sleep, bouts of synchronized activity represent long trajectories called replays.
source: During quiescence and slow wave sleep, bouts of synchronized activity represent long trajectories called replays, which are well-established in place cells and have been recently reported in grid cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental work on replays.

claim: Replays are well-established in place cells.
source: During quiescence and slow wave sleep, bouts of synchronized activity represent long trajectories called replays, which are well-established in place cells and have been recently reported in grid cells.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations.

claim: Replays have been recently reported in grid cells.
source: During quiescence and slow wave sleep, bouts of synchronized activity represent long trajectories called replays, which are well-established in place cells and have been recently reported in grid cells.
evidence: This is supported by recent experimental reports cited in the manuscript.

claim: Theta sequences and replay are hypothesized to facilitate many cognitive functions.
source: Theta sequences and replay are hypothesized to facilitate many cognitive functions, but their underlying mechanisms are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about hypotheses in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The underlying mechanisms of theta sequences and replay are unknown.
source: Theta sequences and replay are hypothesized to facilitate many cognitive functions, but their underlying mechanisms are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: One mechanism proposed for grid cell formation is the continuous attractor network.
source: One mechanism proposed for grid cell formation is the continuous attractor network.
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work on continuous attractor networks.

claim: The continuous attractor network architecture naturally produces theta sequences and replay as distinct consequences of modulating external input.
source: We demonstrate that this established architecture naturally produces theta sequences and replay as distinct consequences of modulating external input.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by the model simulations presented.

claim: Driving inhibitory interneurons at the theta frequency causes attractor bumps to oscillate in speed and size.
source: Driving inhibitory interneurons at the theta frequency causes attractor bumps to oscillate in speed and size, which gives rise to theta sequences and phase precession, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oscillations in attractor bump speed give rise to theta sequences.
source: Driving inhibitory interneurons at the theta frequency causes attractor bumps to oscillate in speed and size, which gives rise to theta sequences and phase precession, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oscillations in attractor bump size give rise to phase precession.
source: Driving inhibitory interneurons at the theta frequency causes attractor bumps to oscillate in speed and size, which gives rise to theta sequences and phase precession, respectively.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Decreasing input drive to all neurons produces traveling wavefronts of activity that are decoded as replays.
source: Decreasing input drive to all neurons produces traveling wavefronts of activity that are decoded as replays.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Place cells in the hippocampal formation fire at one or a few locations.
source: Place cells in the hippocampal formation fire at one or a few locations (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire at many locations that form a triangular lattice in space.
source: grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) fire at many locations that form a triangular lattice in space (Hafting et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: At short timescales, spatially tuned neurons fire in coordinated sequences that represent trajectories away from the current animal position.
source: However, at short timescales, these neurons fire in coordinated sequences that represent trajectories away from the current animal position.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations cited in the manuscript.

claim: The local field potential (LFP) of the hippocampal region is dominated by an oscillation of 5–11 Hz (theta range) when the animal is moving.
source: The first type of sequence occurs when the animal is moving and the local field potential (LFP) of the hippocampal region is dominated by an oscillation of 5–11 Hz, the theta range (Vanderwolf, 1969; O'Keefe, 1976; Vinogradova, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: During every cycle of the theta oscillation, neurons corresponding to locations slightly behind the animal fire first, followed by those corresponding to the current location and finally locations ahead of the animal.
source: During every cycle of this oscillation, neurons corresponding to locations slightly behind the animal fire first, followed by those corresponding to the current location and finally locations ahead of the animal (Skaggs et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Theta sequences involving many neurons are related to a single-neuron phenomenon called phase precession.
source: These so-called theta sequences involving many neurons are related to a single-neuron phenomenon called phase precession (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: When an animal first enters the firing field of a place or grid cell, the neuron spikes late in the theta cycle.
source: When an animal first enters the firing field of a place or grid cell, the neuron spikes late in the theta cycle.
evidence: This is a description of phase precession supported by experimental observations.

claim: As the animal moves through the field, subsequent spikes tend to arrive at smaller theta phase, or earlier within a cycle.
source: As the animal moves through the field, subsequent spikes tend to arrive at smaller theta phase, or earlier within a cycle.
evidence: This is a description of phase precession supported by experimental observations.

claim: Activity within each theta cycle starts with neurons whose peak firing occurs behind the animal and ends with neurons whose peak firing occurs ahead of the animal, which is a theta sequence.
source: Thus, activity within each theta cycle starts with neurons whose peak firing occurs behind the animal and ends with neurons whose peak firing occurs ahead of the animal, which is a theta sequence (Skaggs et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: During idle periods, the LFP of the hippocampal region loses theta oscillations but is instead intermittently punctuated by sharp-wave ripples with power across 140–200 Hz.
source: During idle periods, the LFP of the hippocampal region loses theta oscillations but is instead intermittently punctuated by sharp-wave ripples with power across 140–200 Hz (Buzsáki, 1986; Chrobak and Buzsáki, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: During sharp-wave ripples, spatially tuned neurons fire in coordinated bursts that represent rapid, long-distance trajectories.
source: During these events, spatially tuned neurons fire in coordinated bursts that represent rapid, long-distance trajectories.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of replay.

claim: Replays are well-established in place cells.
source: These replays are well-established in place cells (Lee and Wilson, 2002; Foster and Wilson, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Replays have recently been observed in grid cells within superficial layers of the MEC.
source: and have recently been observed in grid cells within superficial layers of the MEC (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Replays can also involve grid cells within deep layers of the MEC.
source: Note that replays can also involve grid cells within deep layers of the MEC (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2016); these findings, which have been disputed (Trimper et al., 2017), will not be addressed by this work.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work, though the authors note it is disputed.

claim: Hippocampal sequences facilitate many cognitive functions, such as memory consolidation, credit assignment, and action planning.
source: These findings suggest that hippocampal sequences facilitate many cognitive functions, such as memory consolidation, credit assignment, and action planning (Foster, 2017; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018; Zielinski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reviews and experimental work.

claim: The mechanisms that produce theta sequences and replay among place and grid cells are still unclear.
source: However, the mechanisms that produce theta sequences and replay among place and grid cells are still unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The continuous attractor model for producing grid cells has been accumulating experimental support.
source: Meanwhile, a mechanism for producing grid cells themselves, the continuous attractor model, has been accumulating experimental support (Couey et al., 2013; Yoon et al., 2013; Heys et al., 2014; Dunn et al., 2015; Fuchs et al., 2016; Zutshi et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Continuous attractor networks posit particular configurations of synapses within the MEC that are local and symmetric.
source: This class of networks posits particular configurations of synapses within the MEC that are local and symmetric (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Widloski and Fiete, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited theoretical work.

claim: By incorporating fully spiking neural dynamics, new phenomena emerge in the continuous attractor architecture.
source: By incorporating key biological features such as fully spiking neural dynamics, we find that new phenomena emerge in this recurrent architecture: grid cells will exhibit either theta sequences or replays depending on the external input provided by other brain regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Grid cells will exhibit either theta sequences or replays depending on the external input provided by other brain regions.
source: By incorporating key biological features such as fully spiking neural dynamics, we find that new phenomena emerge in this recurrent architecture: grid cells will exhibit either theta sequences or replays depending on the external input provided by other brain regions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The external inputs that determine theta sequences or replays correspond to experimentally measured changes between active and inactive behavior.
source: These inputs correspond to experimentally measured changes between active and inactive behavior (Steriade et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2006) and do not involve changes in connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The external inputs that determine theta sequences or replays do not involve changes in connectivity.
source: These inputs correspond to experimentally measured changes between active and inactive behavior (Steriade et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2006) and do not involve changes in connectivity.
evidence: This is a feature of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The same architecture that produces grid cells causes them to participate in sequences that may be leveraged by other brain regions, such as the hippocampus, to pursue desired cognitive goals.
source: From this perspective, the same architecture that produces grid cells causes them to participate in sequences that may be leveraged by other brain regions, such as the hippocampus, to pursue desired cognitive goals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the model's findings.

claim: The model simulates a single grid module—that is, grid cells of one scale and orientation.
source: We simulate a single grid module—that is, grid cells of one scale and orientation (Stensola et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: The model is based on a continuous attractor network from Burak and Fiete (2009) and Widloski and Fiete (2014).
source: with a continuous attractor network based on Burak and Fiete (2009) and Widloski and Fiete (2014).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: Neurons are assembled in a 2D sheet with five overlapping populations, of which four represent excitatory principal cells and one represents inhibitory interneurons.
source: Neurons are assembled in a 2D sheet with five overlapping populations, of which four represent excitatory principal cells and one represents inhibitory interneurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Each excitatory neuron excites its neighbors across all populations.
source: Each excitatory neuron excites its neighbors across all populations, and each inhibitory neuron inhibits only excitatory neurons located a certain distance away.
evidence: This is a description of the model connectivity.

claim: Each inhibitory neuron inhibits only excitatory neurons located a certain distance away.
source: Each excitatory neuron excites its neighbors across all populations, and each inhibitory neuron inhibits only excitatory neurons located a certain distance away.
evidence: This is a description of the model connectivity.

claim: The model implements fully spiking grid cells that obey leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics.
source: To accurately simulate rapid sequences of spikes, we implement fully spiking grid cells that obey leaky integrate-and-fire dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: Each neuron has a membrane potential that tends toward a steady-state value called the drive.
source: Each neuron has a membrane potential that tends toward a steady-state value called the drive, which represents a combination of resting potential and broad input from other brain regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: If the membrane potential exceeds a threshold of 1 in arbitrary units, a spike is emitted, the potential is reset to 0, and the neuron's targets experience a postsynaptic jump in potential after a brief synaptic delay.
source: If the potential exceeds a threshold of 1 in arbitrary units, a spike is emitted, the potential is reset to 0, and the neuron's targets experience a postsynaptic jump in potential after a brief synaptic delay.
evidence: This is a description of the model dynamics.

claim: During locomotion, excitatory principal cells are driven to fire by various cortical and subcortical inputs.
source: During locomotion, excitatory principal cells are driven to fire by various cortical and subcortical inputs (Kerr et al., 2007; Bonnevie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Excitatory principal cells have drive that exceeds threshold at the center of the neural sheet and decays towards the edges to avoid edge effects that disrupt continuous attractor dynamics.
source: Thus, their drive exceeds threshold at the center of the neural sheet; it decays towards the edges to avoid edge effects that disrupt continuous attractor dynamics (Burak and Fiete, 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, with citation to prior work.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons have subthreshold drive that oscillates at a theta frequency of 8 Hz due to input from the medial septum.
source: Meanwhile, inhibitory interneurons have subthreshold drive that oscillates at a theta frequency of 8 Hz due to input from the medial septum (Brandon et al., 2011; Koenig et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Sulser et al., 2014; Unal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, supported by cited experimental work.

claim: With the model architecture and random initial membrane potentials, the neural sheet naturally develops local regions of activity, called bumps, that are arranged in a triangular lattice and are coherent across populations.
source: With this architecture and random initial membrane potentials, the neural sheet naturally develops local regions of activity, called bumps, that are arranged in a triangular lattice and are coherent across populations (Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 1C and Figure 1—video 1.

claim: The self-organized grid is an attractor state of the network.
source: This self-organized grid is an attractor state of the network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model behavior.

claim: The four excitatory populations each correspond to a perpendicular direction along the neural sheet and a perpendicular direction in the spatial environment.
source: This transformation is performed by the four excitatory populations, each of which corresponds to a perpendicular direction along the neural sheet and a perpendicular direction in the spatial environment.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: Excitatory neurons have output synapses biased in their preferred sheet direction.
source: Excitatory neurons have output synapses biased in their preferred sheet direction (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is a description of the model connectivity, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Excitatory neurons receive more input when the animal moves along their preferred spatial direction.
source: and they receive more input when the animal moves along their preferred spatial direction.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: When the animal moves along a direction, neurons in the corresponding population have increased drive and the activity pattern moves in the corresponding direction on the neural sheet.
source: When the animal moves along, say, the 'North' direction, neurons in the N population have increased drive; since their outputs are biased in the 'up' direction on the neural sheet, the activity pattern moves up.
evidence: This is a description of the model behavior.

claim: The activity pattern on the sheet moves synchronously with the animal's 2D trajectory.
source: In this way, the activity pattern on the sheet moves synchronously with the animal's 2D trajectory (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The grid pattern is projected onto single neuron spatial responses.
source: and the grid pattern is projected onto single neuron spatial responses (Figure 1E and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 1E and Figure 1—video 2.

claim: Each active neuron in the sheet is a grid cell with the same scale and orientation.
source: Each active neuron in the sheet is a grid cell with the same scale and orientation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Over the course of a simulation, the grid-like pattern on the neural sheet drifts such that for a given track position, the corresponding bump locations on the neural sheet slowly change.
source: But over the course of a simulation, the grid-like pattern on the neural sheet drifts (Burak and Fiete, 2009) such that for a given track position, the corresponding bump locations on the neural sheet slowly change.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, with citation to prior work on drift.

claim: Drift in the grid-like pattern introduces errors in path-integration.
source: This drift introduces errors in path-integration (Hardcastle et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by the cited work.

claim: Path-integration errors are believed to be corrected by allocentric input from border cells, boundary vector cells, or landmark cells.
source: which are believed to be corrected by allocentric input from border cells (Ocko et al., 2018; Keinath et al., 2018), boundary vector cells (Evans et al., 2016), or landmark cells (Raudies and Hasselmo, 2015; Savelli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited theoretical and experimental work.

claim: The model implements brief allocentric corrections.
source: Thus, we implement brief allocentric corrections in our model.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: Attractor bump locations on the neural sheet that correspond to either end of the track are learned during simulation setup.
source: Attractor bump locations on the neural sheet that correspond to either end of the track are learned during simulation setup.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: Learned attractor bump locations are periodically reintroduced during the main simulation as excitatory input between idle periods and runs.
source: They are periodically reintroduced during the main simulation as excitatory input between idle periods and runs (Figure 2A,B; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, supported by Figure 2A,B.

claim: Grid cells at different locations in the sheet generally correspond to different positions along the track.
source: Grid cells at different locations in the sheet generally correspond to different positions along the track (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 2C.

claim: From four regions in the sheet chosen for recording, up to 150 excitatory neurons are selected whose spatial firing fields are stable from lap to lap and collectively tile the track.
source: From four regions in the sheet chosen for recording, we select up to 150 excitatory neurons whose spatial firing fields are stable from lap to lap and collectively tile the track (Figure 2D; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the model analysis procedure, supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Over replicate simulations with different random initial membrane potentials, many simulations contain only grid cells with single fields.
source: Over replicate simulations with different random initial membrane potentials, many simulations contain only grid cells with single fields as in Figure 2D.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: In other replicate simulations, the attractor grid self-organizes on the neural sheet with an orientation such that two attractor bumps pass over recorded neurons and produce two fields.
source: In other replicates, the attractor grid self-organizes on the neural sheet with an orientation such that two attractor bumps pass over recorded neurons and produce two fields (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Grid cells in O'Neill et al. (2017) often possess a single dominant field along an arm of a T-maze.
source: Similarly, the grid cells in O'Neill et al. (2017), with which we will primarily compare our results, often possess a single dominant field along an arm of a T-maze.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: At the theta timescale, grid cell activity is highest when the oscillating inhibitory drive is lowest and excitatory cells are most disinhibited.
source: At the theta timescale, grid cell activity is highest when the oscillating inhibitory drive is lowest and excitatory cells are most disinhibited (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Experimentally, grid cells and place cells are most active at troughs of the theta-filtered LFP.
source: Experimentally, grid cells (Hafting et al., 2008) and place cells (Buzsáki, 2002; Feng et al., 2015) are most active at troughs of the theta-filtered LFP
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The experimental observation that grid cells and place cells are most active at troughs of the theta-filtered LFP can be explained in terms of extracellular currents generated by neural activity.
source: which can be explained in terms of extracellular currents generated by neural activity (Buzsáki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited work.

claim: O'Neill et al. (2017) define theta cycles to span from trough to trough of the LFP.
source: O'Neill et al. (2017) define theta cycles to span from trough to trough of the LFP.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methodology in the cited work.

claim: The model aligns theta cycles to start with phase 0° at troughs of the inhibitory drive.
source: Accordingly, we align our theta cycles to start with phase 0° at troughs of the inhibitory drive (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a description of the model analysis procedure, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: During runs, activity passes through recorded neurons as attractor bumps move along the neural sheet.
source: During runs, activity passes through recorded neurons as attractor bumps move along the neural sheet (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Video 1.

claim: Spike trains from single neurons exhibit finer temporal organization with respect to the theta oscillation in a variety of ways.
source: However, spike trains from single neurons exhibit finer temporal organization with respect to the theta oscillation in a variety of ways (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Many neurons are phase-independent and fire throughout the theta cycle.
source: Many neurons are phase-independent and fire throughout the theta cycle.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Some neurons are phase-locking and strongly prefer to fire at 360° (equivalently, 0° or 720°).
source: Some are phase-locking and strongly prefer to fire at 360° (equivalently, 0° or 720°).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Some neurons exhibit phase precession with a preferred phase that starts around 360° when the animal enters a grid field but decreases as the animal progresses through it.
source: Finally, some exhibit phase precession with a preferred phase that starts around 360° when the animal enters a grid field but decreases as the animal progresses through it.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The model's correlation magnitudes 0.17 ± 0.11 (mean ± s.d.) are low compared to experiments, which report grid cells with mean ≈0.3 and place cells with mean ≈0.4.
source: Our correlation magnitudes 0.17 ± 0.11 (mean ± s.d.; Figure 3C) are low compared to experiments, which report grid cells with mean ≈0.3 and place cells with mean ≈0.4 (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results (Figure 3C) with experimental data from the cited work.

claim: The difference in correlation magnitudes between the model and experiments arises from two sources.
source: This difference arises from two sources.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Figure S10 of O'Neill et al. (2017) shows some highly correlated neurons with magnitudes up to 0.8, which are absent from the model simulations.
source: Figure S10 of O'Neill et al. (2017) shows some highly correlated neurons with magnitudes up to 0.8; these are absent from our simulations.
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work.

claim: Figure S10 of O'Neill et al. (2017) shows fewer neurons with correlation value close to 0, which corresponds to either phase-independent or phase-locking neurons.
source: It also shows fewer neurons with correlation value close to 0, which corresponds to either phase-independent or phase-locking neurons.
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work.

claim: Circular-linear correlation cannot distinguish between phase-independent and phase-locking neurons.
source: Since both subgroups lack a preferred theta phase that consistently changes with position, circular-linear correlation cannot distinguish between them (Figure 3B, top two rows).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results, supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Circular-linear regression can differentiate between all three subgroups of phase relationships (phase-independent, phase-locking, and phase-precessing).
source: To further characterize phase behavior, we use circular-linear regression (Kempter et al., 2012), which can differentiate between all three subgroups of phase relationships presented in Figure 3B.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used, with citation.

claim: Phase-independent neurons are defined to have a regression fit score less than a cutoff of 0.4.
source: Phase-independent neurons are defined to have a regression fit score less than a cutoff of 0.4 (Figure 3D; Equation 11).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used.

claim: Neurons with high fit score are distinguished as either phase-locking or precessing by the absolute value of their regression slope in units of field size, which is called the phase precession range.
source: Neurons with high fit score are then distinguished as either phase-locking or precessing by the absolute value of their regression slope in units of field size, which is called the phase precession range (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used, supported by Figure 3E.

claim: A phase precession range of 60° is used as the cutoff to distinguish phase-locking from phase-precessing neurons.
source: We use a range of 60° as the cutoff.
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method used.

claim: Experimentally, phase-locking and precessing neurons are found in Layers III and II (LIII and LII), respectively.
source: Experimentally, phase-locking and precessing neurons are found in Layers III and II (LIII and LII), respectively (Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: A wide variety of phase precession ranges are reported across subtypes of LII neurons with medians spanning from 50° for pyramidal cells to 170° for stellate cells.
source: A wide variety of phase precession ranges are reported across subtypes of LII neurons with medians spanning from 50° for pyramidal cells (Ebbesen et al., 2016) to 170° for stellate cells (Reifenstein et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The cutoff of 60° for phase precession range is close to the lower limit of the span of experimentally reported ranges.
source: Our cutoff is close to the lower limit of this span.
evidence: This is a comparison of the model analysis method with experimental data.

claim: Regardless of the cutoff value, regression slopes are biased towards negative values for rightward laps and positive values for leftward laps, which means that the preferred firing phase tends to decrease as an animal moves through a grid field.
source: Yet, regardless of the cutoff value, regression slopes are biased towards negative values for rightward laps and positive values for leftward laps, which means that the preferred firing phase tends to decrease as an animal moves through a grid field.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The directional tendency of phase precession is a key biological feature seen experimentally.
source: This directional tendency is a key biological feature of phase precession seen experimentally (Hafting et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The directional tendency of phase precession is maintained for other cutoff values applied to the fit score.
source: and it is also maintained for other cutoff values applied to the fit score (Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4A,B.

claim: Phase-locking neurons have a preferred phase around 360° throughout the field.
source: These plots show that phase-locking neurons have a preferred phase around 360° throughout the field
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: Phase-precessing neurons have a preferred phase around 360° at field entry.
source: and that phase-precessing neurons have a preferred phase also around 360° at field entry.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: The preferred phase of 360° at field entry corresponds to theta troughs when excitatory neurons are most disinhibited and matches measurements for LIII and LII neurons.
source: This value corresponds to theta troughs when excitatory neurons are most disinhibited (Figure 2E) and matches measurements for LIII and LII neurons (Hafting et al., 2008; note that their phase convention differs from ours by 180°).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The peak density of phase-precessing neurons decreases by ≈75° over the first 50% of field progress.
source: More detailed features also seem to agree between phase-precessing neurons in our simulations and LII neurons in experiments. First, the peak density decreases by ≈75° over the first 50% of field progress
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: There is a smaller density at around 60% field progress and 140° theta phase in phase-precessing neurons.
source: and second, there is a smaller density at around 60% field progress and 140° theta phase (Figure 3F; Hafting et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work, supported by Figure 3F.

claim: The second density in phase-precessing neurons has been separately related to bursting and a second source of neural input.
source: This second density has been separately related to bursting (Climer et al., 2013) and a second source of neural input (Yamaguchi et al., 2002; Chance, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by the cited work.

claim: Phase precession statistics do not depend on the direction of animal motion.
source: Phase precession statistics do not depend on the direction of animal motion (Figure 3–Figure Supplement 5E,F)
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3–Figure Supplement 5E,F.

claim: In experiments, Climer et al. (2013) report omnidirectional precession in a 2D environment.
source: in experiments, Climer et al. (2013) report omnidirectional precession in a 2D environment.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: Precession range and correlation magnitude increase with animal speed.
source: Precession range and correlation magnitude increase with animal speed (Figure 3–Figure Supplement 6A, p = 0.002 and 0.0006 for precession range and correlation magnitude, respectively, by pooling data across track orientations and applying the Krushal-Wallis H test)
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3–Figure Supplement 6A.

claim: In experiments, Jeewajee et al. (2014) report that faster motion is associated with steeper precession slopes and higher correlation magnitudes.
source: in experiments, Jeewajee et al. (2014) report that faster motion is associated with steeper precession slopes and higher correlation magnitudes (Figure 3a, results for pdcd, which corresponds to field progress defined in this paper).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

source: To summarize our phase precession results, our simulation produces a subgroup of phase-locking neurons akin to MEC LIII neurons and a subgroup of phase-precessing neurons akin to MEC LII neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the model findings.

claim: Higher inhibitory drive suppresses the activity of the excitatory grid cells and decreases the size of bumps.
source: Higher inhibitory drive suppresses the activity of the excitatory grid cells and decreases the size of bumps (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 4A,B.

claim: As an attractor bump moves, its size oscillates with inhibitory drive.
source: As an attractor bump moves, its size oscillates with inhibitory drive (Figure 4C, top, and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 4C and Figure 4—video 1.

claim: The activity bump will most likely first reach a grid cell when it is large and growing in size, which corresponds to the end of the theta cycle when the inhibitory drive is decreasing towards its lowest point.
source: The activity bump will most likely first reach the grid cell when it is large and growing in size, which corresponds to the end of the theta cycle when the inhibitory drive is decreasing towards its lowest point.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: As an animal enters a grid field, the first spike will likely have large theta phase slightly less than 360°.
source: Thus, as an animal enters a grid field, the first spike will likely have large theta phase slightly less than 360°.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: During the next theta cycle, the center of the bump has moved closer to the neuron, so the edge of the bump will reach the neuron when it is growing in size but not as large, and the next spike will have slightly smaller theta phase.
source: During the next theta cycle, the center of the bump has moved closer to the neuron, so the edge of the bump will reach the neuron when it is growing in size but not as large. Thus, the next spike will have slightly smaller theta phase.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Bump size oscillations are the origin of phase precession in the model.
source: This is the origin of phase precession in our model.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Bump oscillations alone can explain the direction of phase precession and the preferred phase at field entry, but spike phases do not decrease perfectly linearly with progress through the field.
source: Thus, bump oscillations alone can explain the direction of phase precession and the preferred phase at field entry, but spike phases do not decrease perfectly linearly with progress through the field.
evidence: This is a finding from the conceptual model presented in Figure 4C.

claim: By explicitly rescaling the activity of the average bump without otherwise changing its time-varying shape, neurons enriched in one of the phase relationships (phase-locking, phase-precessing, or phase-independent) can be generated.
source: By explicitly rescaling the activity of the average bump without otherwise changing its time-varying shape, we can generate neurons enriched in one of these phase relationships (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the simplified model presented in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Under high activity, neurons are driven to fire across all theta phases and exhibit phase independence.
source: Under high activity, neurons are driven to fire across all theta phases and exhibit phase independence.
evidence: This is a finding from the simplified model.

claim: Under low activity, neurons only fire during the most permissive theta phase and exhibit phase locking at 360°.
source: Under low activity, neurons only fire during the most permissive theta phase and exhibit phase locking at 360°.
evidence: This is a finding from the simplified model.

claim: Under intermediate levels of activity, neurons can respond to oscillations in bump size and exhibit phase precession.
source: Under intermediate levels of activity, neurons can respond to oscillations in bump size as demonstrated in Figure 4C and exhibit phase precession.
evidence: This is a finding from the simplified model, supported by Figure 4C.

claim: The finding that activity level influences phase behavior is supported by the experimental report that higher spike counts are associated with steeper precession slopes.
source: This finding on how activity level influences phase behavior is supported by the experimental report that higher spike counts are associated with steeper precession slopes (Jeewajee et al., 2014, Figure 3b, results for pdcd, which corresponds to field progress defined in this paper).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: In the main model, neurons with low, medium, and high firing rates have increased likelihoods for phase locking, precession, and independence.
source: Our main model also reflects this finding: neurons with low, medium, and high firing rates have increased likelihoods for phase locking, precession, and independence (Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the main model simulations, supported by Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4D.

claim: The heterogeneous phase behaviors observed in the main simulations arise, at least in part, from heterogeneous levels of bump activity.
source: Thus, the heterogeneous phase behaviors observed in our main simulations arise, at least in part, from heterogeneous levels of bump activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Three factors that determine the level of activity experienced by a neuron are its distance to the center of the neural sheet, its sheet location relative to attractor bumps, and its preferred firing direction relative to animal motion.
source: Three factors that determine the level of activity experienced by a neuron are its distance to the center of the neural sheet, its sheet location relative to attractor bumps, and its preferred firing direction relative to animal motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: The prevalence of different phase behaviors varies with distance to the center of the neural sheet, sheet location relative to attractor bumps, and preferred firing direction relative to animal motion.
source: Accordingly, the prevalence of different phase behaviors varies with these factors (Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4E,G and Figure 3–Figure Supplement 5B,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 3–Figure Supplement 4E,G and Figure 3–Figure Supplement 5B,D.

claim: The decoded position generally matches the animal's actual position.
source: The decoded position generally matches the animal's actual position (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the theta timescale, there are deviations in decoded position whose regularities are revealed by averaging over theta cycles.
source: but at the theta timescale, there are deviations whose regularities are revealed by averaging over theta cycles.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Within each theta cycle, the decoded position increases rapidly, before retreating at cycle boundaries.
source: However, within each theta cycle, the decoded position increases rapidly, before retreating at cycle boundaries.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 5B.

claim: The forward sweeps in decoded position are identified as theta sequences.
source: We identify these forward sweeps as theta sequences
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Theta sequences represent motion at 0.88 ± 0.15 m/s, approximately twice the actual speed of 0.50 ± 0.05 m/s (mean ± s.d.).
source: which represent motion at 0.88 ± 0.15 m/s, approximately twice the actual speed of 0.50 ± 0.05 m/s (mean ± s.d.; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 5C.

claim: The theta sequence speed of approximately twice the actual speed matches experimental observations of average theta sequence speed ≈1 m/s compared to the animal's speed of ≈0.4–0.5 m/s.
source: This matches experimental observations of average theta sequence speed ≈1 m/s compared to the animal's speed of ≈0.4–0.5 m/s (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work.

claim: Theta sequences, like phase precession, arise naturally in the model from an effect of oscillating inhibitory drive on attractor bumps.
source: Theta sequences, like phase precession, arise naturally in our model from an effect of oscillating inhibitory drive on attractor bumps.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Inhibitory drive affects the speed at which bumps move along the neural sheet—higher inhibitory drive produces faster bump motion for a given animal speed.
source: In addition to determining bump size, inhibitory drive also affects the speed at which bumps move along the neural sheet—higher inhibitory drive produces faster bump motion for a given animal speed (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 6A,B.

claim: At the middle of theta cycles, inhibitory drive is highest, so attractor bumps move quickly and represent fast animal trajectories.
source: At the middle of theta cycles, inhibitory drive is highest, so attractor bumps move quickly and represent fast animal trajectories.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Theta sequences are faster than the animal's actual speed, which is approximately constant within a theta cycle and thus encoded as the average bump speed over the entire cycle.
source: These theta sequences are faster than the animal's actual speed, which is approximately constant within a theta cycle and thus encoded as the average bump speed over the entire cycle.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The location of peak activity in the average attractor bump moves with a sawtooth-like pattern that, over a theta cycle, lags behind the overall motion of the bump and advances ahead of it.
source: The location of peak activity moves with a sawtooth-like pattern that, over a theta cycle, lags behind the overall motion of the bump and advances ahead of it (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of average bump dynamics, supported by Figure 6D.

claim: The forward surges in peak activity location produce the sequences in decoded position.
source: These forward surges produce the sequences in decoded position (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism, supported by Figure 5D.

claim: The model's mechanism for theta sequences can explain why their speed is roughly twice the actual speed, as observed experimentally.
source: Our model's mechanism for theta sequences can explain why their speed is roughly twice the actual speed, as observed experimentally (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism, with comparison to experimental data.

claim: If the theta oscillation spends roughly the same amount of time at its peaks (when attractor bumps move at maximal speed) and at its troughs (when bumps do not move at all), then the average bump speed (which encodes the actual animal speed) is half the maximal bump speed (which encodes the theta sequence speed).
source: Suppose the theta oscillation spends roughly the same amount of time at its peaks, when attractor bumps move at maximal speed, and at its troughs, when bumps do not move at all. Then, the average bump speed, which encodes the actual animal speed, is half the maximal bump speed, which encodes the theta sequence speed.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Simulations with different configurations all have theta sequence speeds between 1.2 and 2.5 times the actual speed.
source: Indeed, simulations whose grid cells contain two fields, whose track is oriented differently, whose trajectory is faster or slower, or whose parameters are chosen differently all have theta sequence speeds between 1.2 and 2.5 times the actual speed (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The neocortex, which activates MEC principal cells, is broadly less active during slow wave sleep.
source: The neocortex, which activates MEC principal cells, is broadly less active during slow wave sleep (Steriade et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The medial septum, which inhibits MEC interneurons, increases its firing rate while losing most of its oscillatory nature during slow wave sleep.
source: and the medial septum, which inhibits MEC interneurons, increases its firing rate while losing most of its oscillatory nature (Simon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work.

claim: The model represents the effects of slow wave sleep as decreased excitatory drive and decreased inhibitory drive without oscillations.
source: We model these effects respectively as decreased excitatory drive and decreased inhibitory drive without oscillations (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, supported by Figure 7A.

claim: The network rapidly switches between inputs representing the active state and those representing quiescence as the animal transitions between quiescence and runs.
source: The network rapidly switches between these inputs and those of Figure 1B, which represent the active state, as the animal transitions between quiescence and runs.
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation.

claim: During idle periods, attractor bumps still form a lattice at the center of the neural sheet, where excitatory drive still exceeds threshold.
source: During quiescence, attractor bumps still form a lattice at the center of the neural sheet, where excitatory drive still exceeds threshold (Figure 7B and Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7B and Video 1.

claim: During idle periods, attractor bumps vanish toward the edge of the sheet, where they are replaced by traveling wavefronts of activity.
source: However, these bumps vanish toward the edge of the sheet, where they are replaced by traveling wavefronts of activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Wavefronts cannot be solely sustained by excitatory drive, which is subthreshold in the outer region; instead, they must be nucleated and then self-sustained through excitatory-to-excitatory connections.
source: These wavefronts cannot be solely sustained by excitatory drive, which is subthreshold in this outer region; instead, they must be nucleated and then self-sustained through excitatory-to-excitatory connections.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: In the model, nucleation of wavefronts occurs at activity bumps toward the edge of the sheet.
source: In our model, nucleation occurs at activity bumps toward the edge of the sheet (Video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Video 1.

claim: Once nucleated, the wavefront propagates freely through the outer region because inhibitory neurons, with low drive, are not activated by the wavefront.
source: Once nucleated, the wavefront propagates freely through the outer region because inhibitory neurons, with low drive, are not activated by the wavefront.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: Wavefronts cannot propagate in the center region, because excitatory neurons there receive enough drive to spike vigorously and activate nearby inhibitory neurons.
source: In contrast, wavefronts cannot propagate in the center region, because excitatory neurons there receive enough drive to spike vigorously and activate nearby inhibitory neurons (Figure 7B, inhibitory population).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism, supported by Figure 7B.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons, with their surround distribution of synaptic outputs, constrain neural activity to localized bumps and prevent wavefront propagation in the center region.
source: These interneurons, with their surround distribution of synaptic outputs (Figure 1A), constrain neural activity to localized bumps and prevent wavefront propagation.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism, supported by Figure 1A.

claim: When a wavefront passes through a region of recorded neurons, it can appear as a sequence of spikes that is decoded as a rapid trajectory.
source: When a wavefront passes through a region of recorded neurons, it can appear as a sequence of spikes (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) that is decoded as a rapid trajectory (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rapid trajectories decoded from wavefronts are identified as replays.
source: We identify these events as replays
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results.

claim: Replays traverse much of the track over ~100 ms.
source: which traverse much of the track over ~100 ms (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Due to the stochastic nature of wavefront generation, the number of detected replays can vary considerably across laps and across replicate simulations.
source: Due to the stochastic nature of wavefront generation, the number of detected replays can vary considerably across laps (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and across replicate simulations (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7F.

claim: Replays have a characteristic speed determined by that of wavefront propagation; it is 7.0 ± 2.6 m/s, which is about 14 times faster than the actual speed of 0.50 ± 0.05 m/s (mean ± s.d.).
source: However, replays have a characteristic speed determined by that of wavefront propagation; it is 7.0 ± 2.6 m/s, which is about 14 times faster than the actual speed of 0.50 ± 0.05 m/s (mean ± s.d.; Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7G.

claim: The replay speed of about 14 times the actual speed agrees with experiments, which measure replays at ≈4–6 m/s and actual motion at ≈0.4–0.5 m/s.
source: This agrees with experiments, which measure replays at ≈4–6 m/s and actual motion at ≈0.4–0.5 m/s (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of model results with experimental data from the cited work.

claim: Replay speed depends on the number of grid fields and the values of simulation parameters.
source: Replay speed depends on the number of grid fields and the values of simulation parameters (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Across all simulation parameters and detection methods, replays are always much faster than both the actual animal speed and the theta sequence speed, as observed experimentally.
source: Nevertheless, across all simulation parameters and detection methods, replays are always much faster than both the actual animal speed and the theta sequence speed, as observed experimentally (O'Neill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, with comparison to experimental data from the cited work.

claim: Replays are the fastest network phenomenon because traveling wavefronts lack inhibition.
source: This happens because traveling wavefronts lack inhibition and should be the network phenomenon that propagates fastest.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: With lower velocity gain, attractor bumps travel shorter distances, and there is a clear correspondence between neural sheet location and track position.
source: With lower velocity gain, attractor bumps travel shorter distances, and such a correspondence is apparent (yellow and purple areas in Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8A.

claim: When an animal is idle at either end of the track, attractor bumps are still located at neurons that represent the current position.
source: When an animal is idle at either end of the track, attractor bumps are still located at neurons that represent the current position (Figure 8A and Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8A and Figure 8—video 1.

claim: Replays are nucleated at attractor bumps.
source: Recall that replays are nucleated at attractor bumps (Video 1 and Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations, supported by Video 1 and Figure 8A.

claim: As a wavefront radiates from a bump, it will likely first activate neurons whose firing fields represent nearby positions, followed by those with increasingly distant fields, due to the correspondence between neural sheet locations and track positions.
source: As a wavefront radiates from a bump, it will likely first activate neurons whose firing fields represent nearby positions, followed by those with increasingly distant fields, due to the correspondence between neural sheet locations and track positions (Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8—video 1.

claim: The decoded position tends to start near the actual position of the animal and travel away from it.
source: Thus, the decoded position tends to start near the actual position of the animal and travel away from it (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: The decoded starting position of replays are closer to the actual position than the decoded ending position.
source: Accordingly, the decoded starting position of replays are closer to the actual position than the decoded ending position (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8C.

claim: Despite the predominance of replays directed away from the actual animal position, some start at the opposite side of the track and travel toward the actual position.
source: However, replays are not all detected immediately after wavefront nucleation; wavefronts traveling for some time may pass through a region of recorded neurons from any direction. Thus, despite the predominance of replays directed away from the actual animal position, some start at the opposite side of the track and travel toward the actual position (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with lower velocity gain, supported by Figure 8B.

claim: The directional bias of replays has not been directly assessed for grid cells, but it appears in experiments on hippocampal replay.
source: This directional bias has not been directly assessed for grid cells, but it appears in experiments on hippocampal replay (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental work on hippocampal replay.

claim: With periodic boundaries that eliminate edges, uniform excitatory drive can be implemented during both runs and idle periods.
source: With periodic boundaries that eliminate edges, we can implement uniform excitatory drive during both runs and idle periods (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation with periodic boundary conditions, supported by Figure 8D,E.

claim: With periodic boundary conditions and uniform drive, the entire neural sheet exhibits attractor bumps during runs and activity wavefronts during idle periods.
source: This allows the entire neural sheet to exhibit attractor bumps during runs and activity wavefronts during idle periods (Figure 8F,G and Figure 8—video 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with periodic boundary conditions, supported by Figure 8F,G and Figure 8—video 2.

claim: With periodic boundary conditions and uniform drive, replays can be recorded from anywhere on the neural sheet.
source: Thus, replays can be recorded from anywhere on the neural sheet.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with periodic boundary conditions.

claim: With periodic boundary conditions and uniform drive, allocentric input at the end of each idle period is essential because positional information in the form of attractor bumps completely disappears.
source: Note that allocentric input at the end of each idle period is essential in this case because positional information in the form of attractor bumps completely disappears.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model implementation with periodic boundary conditions.

evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations with periodic boundary conditions, supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: The model unifies phase precession, theta sequences, and replay under a single model while maintaining distinctions among them.
source: We unify phase precession, theta sequences, and replay under a single model while maintaining distinctions among them.
evidence: This is a summary of the model findings.

source: Phase precession and theta sequences arise naturally from oscillations in attractor bump size and speed, respectively, which are both consequences of medial septum input.

claim: It is conceivable that one theta-related phenomenon can exist without the other under certain conditions.

source: Replays in our model arise from the disappearance of attractor bumps and their replacement by traveling wavefronts of activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the model findings.

source: Wavefront propagation involves dynamical processes that are fundamentally different from attractor bump motion, and thus has led to different decoded speeds and directions for replays and theta sequences.

source: Crucially, we produce these phenomena in a continuous attractor network that can still generate 2D grid cells through path integration.

claim: The model implementation shares similarities with an early version of the continuous attractor model (Burak and Fiete, 2009) and a version whose connectivity can be learned (Widloski and Fiete, 2014).
source: Our implementation shares similarities with an early version of the model (Burak and Fiete, 2009) and a version whose connectivity can be learned (Widloski and Fiete, 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, with citations.

claim: The model uses fully spiking neurons, which are rarely used in grid cell attractor models.
source: First, we use fully spiking neurons, which are rarely used in grid cell attractor models—we have only found them utilized in English (2017) and Bush and Burgess (2014), the latter of which combines an attractor network with the oscillatory interference model for grid cells (Burgess et al., 2007; Hasselmo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, with citations.

claim: Typically, neural dynamics in grid cell attractor models are founded on firing rates, which can be used to generate spike trains through a memoryless Poisson process.
source: Typically, neural dynamics are founded on firing rates, which can be used to generate spike trains through a memoryless Poisson process (Burak and Fiete, 2009; Widloski and Fiete, 2014)
evidence: This is a description of typical grid cell attractor models, with citations.

claim: Typical grid cell attractor models do not capture the strong short-time anticorrelation in spiking due to the reset of membrane potential.
source: these models do not capture the strong short-time anticorrelation in spiking due to the reset of membrane potential.
evidence: This is a critique of typical grid cell attractor models.

claim: The model includes excitatory-to-excitatory connections in accordance with their recent experimental discovery.
source: Second, we include excitatory-to-excitatory connections in accordance with their recent experimental discovery (Fuchs et al., 2016; Winterer et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2017; Zutshi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, with citations to experimental work.

claim: Excitatory-to-excitatory connections allow wavefronts to propagate among excitatory neurons while nearby inhibitory neurons remain silent.
source: These connections allow wavefronts to propagate among excitatory neurons while nearby inhibitory neurons remain silent.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model mechanism.

claim: The model varies the external input to the network between active and quiescent behavioral states in accordance with observations.
source: Third, we vary the external input to the network between active and quiescent behavioral states in accordance with observations (Steriade et al., 2001; Simon et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the model implementation, with citations to experimental work.

claim: The network can instantly switch between operating regimes that exhibit either theta-related phenomena or replays.
source: Consequently, the network can instantly switch between operating regimes that exhibit either theta-related phenomena or replays.
evidence: This is a summary of the model findings.

claim: The model presents a distinct conception of entorhinal replay that can be tested experimentally.
source: Our model presents a distinct conception of entorhinal replay that can be tested experimentally.
evidence: This is a statement about the model's testability.

claim: Direct observation of propagating wavefronts can be pursued by calcium imaging of the MEC.
source: Direct observation of propagating wavefronts can be pursued by calcium imaging of the MEC (Heys et al., 2014; Diehl et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental testing, with citations to relevant techniques.

claim: Tetrode recordings of grid cell replay in open field environments may be analyzed for wavefront dynamics.
source: Otherwise, tetrode recordings of grid cell replay in open field environments may be analyzed for wavefront dynamics.
evidence: This is a suggestion for experimental testing.

source: In two dimensions, wavefronts would not represent a single trajectory, but instead a manifold of positions that sweep out a plane through space.
